query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Localized, rapid laser-assisted interfacial re-melting treatment along the lamellar colony boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys will form a nanometer-scale, ductile, coherent interfacial layer that reduces stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, thereby simultaneously improving strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase (fcc/B2) lamellar colonies that contain incoherent internal boundaries acting as stress concentrators.
generation.intervention: Application of a localized, rapid laser-assisted interfacial re-melting process to the colony boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, ductile, and coherent interfacial layer along the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The laser re-melting modifies the local interface structure and chemistry, enhancing interfacial cohesion. This reduces stress concentration at the boundaries and mitigates microcrack nucleation, thus improving load transfer between phases and enabling a simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated, as‐cast state, the laser-treated alloy is expected to exhibit increased yield and fracture strengths as well as improved elongation (ductility) during room-temperature tensile tests.
generation.baseline: Conventional as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with unmodified dual-phase lamellar colonies.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to eutectic HEAs with well‐defined lamellar colonies; the effectiveness depends on precise control of laser parameters (e.g., energy density, pulse duration) to avoid excessive melting or unwanted phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal laser treatment parameters (e.g., interfacial layer thickness and uniformity) and the exact magnitude of improvements in strength and ductility require experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the eutectic HEA: one treated with the localized, rapid laser-assisted interfacial re-melting process and one left in the as-cast state. Characterize the microstructure using TEM/SEM to assess the presence, uniformity, and cohesion of the interfacial layer. Subsequently, perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation, and quantify microcrack density post-deformation.
measurements: Interfacial layer characteristics (thickness, coherence) via TEM/SEM
Yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation from tensile tests
Microcrack distribution and density analysis in deformed samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if the treated interfaces do not show reduced microcrack initiation compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. The reference alloys were chosen because the current EHEA can be regarded as a highly concentrated pseudo-binary NiAl/(Co, Cr, Fe) eutectic alloy, and they are also known to be promising high-temperature alloys, due to the lower density and melting point, much higher thermal conductivity, and excellent oxidation resistance at high temperatures. The major disadvantages for NiAl are the low ductility at room temperature and the low strength at high-temperatures, which also constitute the motivation to develop NiAl/Cr(Mo) eutectic alloys, where the in-situ formed composite structure is expected to improve the mechanical properties of NiAl. As seen in Fig. 6a, compared to NiAl or NiAl/Cr(Mo) eutectic alloys, the EHEA exhibited a much higher fracture strength, and more importantly, a simultaneously much higher ductility at room temperature. A commonly adopted strategy to overcome this strength-ductility tradeoff is to develop multi-phase microstructures, involving at least one ductile/soft and one hard/strong phase, mixed in the appropriate proportion. Common examples include duplex alloys, such as 2205 stainless steel, which have a hard bcc phase to increase the strength of the alloy and a soft fcc phase to maintain the tensile ductility while deformation. The goal has been on fine-tuning the alloy composition and/or processing conditions in order to obtain a material with a good balance between ductility and strength. Eutectic alloys, often exhibiting a two-phase lamellar microstructure, offer such a possibility, and have been investigated for many years in different classes of alloys. Eutectic morphologies are characterized by the simultaneous growth of two (or more) phases from the liquid. A recently developed new class of eutectic HEAs (EHEAs), have attracted a lot of attention due to their promising mechanical properties. decision.trend: Early work established that casting eutectic high-entropy alloys to form fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructures (PMC4145285) already offered a route to attain a balance of strength and ductility. Subsequent studies introduced severe thermomechanical processing – for example, cryo‐rolling followed by annealing (PMC5818523, PMC6353877) – to refine the lamellae and generate heterogeneous or duplex microstructures. These processing routes increased yield strength (via grain/nanostructure refinement, coherent interfaces, and nanoprecipitation) but the ubiquitous dual‐phase lamellar colonies retained numerous internal boundaries that still act as stress concentrators and microcrack initiators under room-temperature tensile loading.
decision.unsolved: Although processing routes have evolved to enhance strength–ductility synergy, the fundamental weakness remains at the internal colony boundaries. These boundaries, due to their incoherent or weak nature, still promote microcracking that undercuts ductility despite improvements elsewhere in the microstructure.
decision.lever: application of a localized, rapid laser-assisted interfacial re-melting treatment to induce the in situ formation of a thin, ductile, and coherent interfacial layer along the lamellar colony boundaries
decision.why: This approach directly targets the internal boundaries that are the nucleation sites for microcracks by engineering their structure and chemistry without modifying the overall bulk composition. Building on the trend of processing‐based microstructural refinement, a controlled laser melting process can selectively alter the interfacial regions—by promoting the formation of nanometer-scale, ductile films—that both bridge the phases and alleviate stress concentrations. Prior work on thermomechanical treatments has improved overall properties, and similar interface‐engineering strategies in other alloy systems have demonstrated crack-arresting capabilities, making this the most plausible next step. An experiment comparing room-temperature tensile properties and microcrack propagation in laser-treated versus untreated EHEAs would serve to falsify the hypothesis if the interfacial modification fails to reduce microcracking and does not yield simultaneous gains in both strength and ductility.
